![IM-20250702-WA0002[1].jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/macaroth90/23w2o87jCPf26i2ib7ExSmvbNmbHZ8emPZ2mrGEhbn9qe4kNnmrTQbcVMFxj4ZMGmm8Kb.jpg)
After the Mass at the grotto, we walked around a little more to explore what lay behind the basilica. We crossed the bridge and continued sightseeing, but just then, the rain suddenly started pouring. Since it kept getting heavier, we decided to call it a day, as it became difficult to continue walking and enjoying the surroundings.

Before leaving, we quietly said goodbye to the saints and the beautiful sanctuary of Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes.

We then walked back along the same road we had passed earlier and stopped at one of the coffee stands for a warm drink, while my daughter happily enjoyed an ice cream. Earlier that day, we had lunch at an Indian restaurant, though there were also many other restaurants nearby offering different kinds of meals to choose from.

And that concludes our journey to Lourdes—a peaceful and unforgettable experience filled with faith, history, and beautiful memories.

***
My London work plus leisure trip has come to an end as this will be the final post for my UK and London series, thanks to everyone who have followed my colourful journey in this amazing country and city.

In the final post, I wanted to end with the icons of London, especially those that I haven't mentioned, but still deserved a mention. And it starts with a walk along River Thames. In one of first days, I took this walk during the evening, it was quite a nice walk and there was a lot of sights to soak in. And you could see the ferris wheel, London Eye, in the distance.


<center>![20140611_181159.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/2458LVXLeoFkkmcBVK36p2WNuHmXMv2G6MeX2wRAuQwMutnQ4Cioc1RKEmcCnWLhkxPGn.jpg)</center>


<center>![20140611_181548.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/243frBfJYj8XktPDrCWvzrbzGhkzGVyWoFEV6W5zDgieRdrx6vae3ad6nm3nfELKtU7MX.jpg)</center>


They even had bars on the boats on the river. Would people really want to dine on a platform that sways with the waters? Definitely a no no for people with motion sickness.

<center>![20140611_182138.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/23yJCAP7g5GvKXgdtad5jxEZfKcHZeSMpyPZ4hjTukm1nhmKd5mWMTDeBv2uBjSQzPhgb.jpg)</center>

There were many of such bridges on River Thames as we got closer to London Eye.

<center>![20140611_182312.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/245Hj2d38ZQ1eEtdxdU6BRzgMGyvfdUFXQAu2JKGNFiocawMt8MSQew2U8DgXdZmDGNSq.jpg)</center>

Finally we reached! We have a similar one in Singapore, called the Singapore Flyer, so it wasn't a big WOW for me. Still it's nice to look at as the biggest icon in the background of all the photos in this area.

<center>![20140611_183629.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/243WPj1zbx83oE4jZ1tjqVQbNYp6NV3jENtPjP9ZsJqJvTs6ovp2cAxfFHjrfjvD1oWQg.jpg)</center>

<center>![20140614_154909.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/244KRFmyQKJFcCmXN5QXijqaoSXF8CCVNRcbZGwza1wytWWRgzZWdCy2dkkYqnEnsgWzU.jpg)</center>

Another of those bridges as we headed back to the hotel.

<center>![20140611_183909.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/23zRwBEGvK8Pe3vTWjFFwN8btXSRytjrN11vsCgNGVMgFv6spqeZ8fXJxji1qsuQpcf6a.jpg)</center>

If you play Monopoly, you definitely would know this place. Advance to Trafalgar Square! Yes, this is the Trafalgar Square! Very crowded and the building behind is National Gallery.


<center>![20140614_140724.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/23sdbPsCMBkWq2AHL4RDCgTFqEKB9CGLZU8QZBoCnqWWUYFmxnLVGpwtREZ8Lok74yexV.jpg)</center>

Some historical structures spotted in the area too!

<center>![20140614_140534.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/242rsK8BhWcKaVt8xhS8vk6Qngp7nG4cVUD7UM2bum2ohvMXfhcj875Dk1ySF18fjbbmu.jpg)</center>


<center>![20140614_140530.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/23qrLVcCuYvp2aX8r5ND3H75V2V25Vx1yYYy7U5CD6hGcfwGdy1h9gQNfUMkdtQtRZaEq.jpg)</center>

And within walking distance, we arrived at the Big Ben!

<center>![20140614_153353.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/242NgxN4E8qw39YJQk5pogKSjrqJGocTccbW5PMWhhMPJtWHsHRZmociW1gUpPLsqYdwN.jpg)</center>

And that's the Palace of Westminister, which is the meeting place for their Parliament.

<center>![20140614_154641.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/241EzmTXWTM4hdn9hFfvKZPpZakbriEZ9CYzn5hvANar98dJNP4E2mEvAZioQqv19Gd1C.jpg)</center>

Another must visit in London is British Museum! The museum was so big, and I was there on two occasions and I think I didn't manage to cover the entire museum. Here's one of the beautiful halls.



<center>![20140612_170209.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/23xefTGEwPwwbjii5PF8PSAj3RohUEbQYWdLUMTeeTBhBeXpsbHf3bGuGSr8HuF9oxRg9.jpg)</center>


<center>![20140612_181119.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/23ynWt3TcPvbUjvuc2uocpA2TjvJhTXzucagDpZuyZzPdy7BRk5pR9qZTRcAFbyQiPpra.jpg)</center>


<center>![20140612_181058.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/23yws7JHWcy1J2M6gfSVuRN6tZeFjdt8ataQ7K9CC37MzPSAioTdbR14XDJhqpqdz95zQ.jpg)</center>

Finally, a "tourist attraction". Not so much of an attraction but there were long lines of crowds queueing up to take photo at "Platform 9 3/4". If you are a Harry Potter fan, you would know how iconic this trolley and platform is.

<center>![20140614_164143.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/23xVKEAHFG3fq7dL45Yv2ggzAf9t3Xmnm5DovasZqj4RU1R4j7zTMKiNQzWUxbCa5CwGG.jpg)</center>


<center>![20140614_164308.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/23zbRq4hhSgC1UWPjPxV6KaLmyGBLAs2Q89qjgGhKaVJ2wBDnz6PKSPUFsi2ikcmPPEDT.jpg)</center>

They also had a shop which sells Harry Potter merchandise, and of course, it was very crowded as well.

<center>![20140614_165007.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/243BkPVqrqtaicA4vb7e7QGgjTCg3xvh7njVN1GpAWfoyd1kThLfZBC89iQskiDRNKxJp.jpg)</center>


It's been so many years, but definitely brings back memories. I read all their books and watched all the movies, have you?

<center>![20140614_165321.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/23wgFgJ6EtMppZtBEJ82sJzZg6uLTnCnLqH16vGUzJ6Qfu7iKBg37KEDR5XVxvefKnksr.jpg)</center>

I was tempted to buy those T-shirts because the me 12 years ago felt there were too expensive. Haha.

<center>![20140614_170316.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/relf87/23vhwjCTiNPbonieiNsRTejfcLprckUKeZDi8RoWWf5C7T33zomM2ErZjDpqmi7eZFk9x.jpg)</center>

So that's it! 13 posts and a few thousands of words! My posts for the London trip are complete! To be honest, I didn't expect there were so many things to write about, but as I got through the posts and photos, there was indeed a lot of rave about UK and London! So where should we go to next? ;)


And that's all I have today! Have you been to London or United Kingdom? Let me know in the comments below!

Finally, thanks for reading my post in the community under World Map Pin!

It’s quite disorientating, or perhaps weirdly orientating, being in Tasmania.

If you open Google Maps, that little blue dot puts you as close to Antarctica as you’re ever likely to get unless you’ve got a heap of money for a tour down there, which, admittedly, would be pretty incredible. Anyone wanna lend me $20K Australian? If you come from the south of Australia, chances are you've looked out to see a *lot* and imagined that almost mythical icy land mass. You might have even known people to work out there. Admired the Sea Shephard fighting Japanese whalers in its surrounding waters. 


I do love this cold southern ocean. There’s a feeling of standing at the edge of things, like the world just runs out if you keep going south. But it’s not just empty. There’s movement out there too, animals and people, waves, wind, saltstreams. 


![2383.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/riverflows/23sdbK8wsgGMp87pYw4HJf4ChGm8TSdmbzb1nkmSYPDePv4MEwZqBoGYmZb1DXRG1tpeG.jpg)


Every so often, ships pass through - icebreakers and research vessels making their way back from Antarctica toward Hobart. You can stand on a quiet beach and watch something that’s just come from the bottom of the world, cutting a slow line across the horizon. There's sailboats too, breezing along, seals, dolphins, seabirds, clouds. The low Autumnal sun. 


![2390.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/riverflows/23zRvavNUuKQWK6w8Ehx1BujW9eC9Yrnyxo5gMwDmNZ6eitkienNCpZ1s9pSenuxiDqve.jpg)


Even so, there are more mainlanders here now, and plenty of people moving from the bigger part of Australia chasing something quieter, wilder, more beautiful. A place that still feels like it has space in it, wildness, freedom. People used to leave Tassie to get jobs and go to uni on the mainland and never make it back - now it seems people flock there or return to their roots. There's hikers and explorers and climbers and surfers, people drifting, sailing, fighting for the environment. It feels like a last frontier.

Every time I come here, I end up back in that same feeling: just looking out at the sea and thinking about how far away everything else is. How it'd be easy to be cut off from the mainland if a disaster stopped the planes and boats coming. There's understandable a lot of climate fiction set in Tassie.

Here, we're on Hope’s Beach, on the South Arm, Nipaluna (another word for Hobart), is one of those places you wouldn’t find unless you knew it was there. A dirt track leads you down to a wide stretch of sand that feels tucked away from everything - no asphalted carpark or paid for parking. There’s often surf here, usually big, messy waves even when it’s onshore and a bit chaotic. Not like the calmer beaches on the other side of the bay I’ve written about before - and it's a place local surfers will flock to even if it's tiny, particularly when it's clean and offshore like this weekend. 


![2442.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/riverflows/EqL6L4zmn1QAJNbvN7KDwjNLTWoKTAsZHc4b25e83cFQVii6XE3d5kRrq3D6LpB355r.jpg)



When I go there, it’s usually to watch Tam surf. She’s a strong surfer, much fitter than me, and tends to take on bigger waves without hesitation - her Dad was a big wave surfer. On this particular day though, there’s barely any swell at all. So we just take the dog for a walk and end up swimming in the freezing water anyway. 

It’s icy, a whole 3 degrees colder than home, which makes a difference. Still, it’s refreshing. It knocks the edge off everything, like washing out the red wine from the night before. I tend to just experience cold as a sensation these days not a warning to squeal and get the fuck out. I'm safe, there, held for a moment. 

Tam does end up paddling out into the tiny waves regardless, chasing whatever little ocean fix she can get. I sit on the sand watching, the sun low in the sky all day, warm but with that persistent Tasmanian chill underneath it. The light starts getting afternoony golden way earlier than home - by 3, it feels like it's getting dark. 

The beach is littered with shellsp - pipis, mussels, oyster shells - washed in from the harbour and the bay. We don't know how safe they are to eat, though the air is cleaner than anywhere in teh world.


![2447.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/riverflows/23xybJWqjJv81evNqhnhYvde9cHSSfEbR1dFNn2S8PvXrNzAqMbsrSWTrLH62qQSyZj3h.jpg)

Looking out to sea, Betsy Island sits low on the horizon, just another marker in a chain of land and water that’s always been about passage, but seems like a cool place to have a shack, if you wanted an island off an island off an island and to be totally isolated. I wonder if it is 'owned'.

We bring the dog down because of his separation anxiety. He’s a sweetheart, mostly, but spends a lot of time staring out at the water waiting for Tam to come back in, and barely tolerates me. Though he does eventually decide I’m useful enough to carry him up the sanddune because he does have very short legs and he is very, very old.


![b384e77d-7665-4142-bdf7-633989d2a67d-1_all_26838.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/riverflows/Eqd7zuopbaETYnHBEVF56Vza22vcVJuqwHTY4L9w6ocwef8SL2V1ueaJzL4nzezePbm.jpg)


On the walk back, black cockatoos move through the pines, breaking open cones. There's more than I've ever seen in one place before - some forty of them, making a noise and chucking pine cones. 

I love Tassie, so much.

result.body: ![](https://images.ecency.com/DQmPzQdW8ZSfTrcB4tz1itqreFAj2ZK2V3EqicT8bm3jPSh/ff.jpg) Hello, friends and the #WednesdayWalk community! Happy Wednesday to all of you. We’ve recently traveled from the tropics to the Northern Hemisphere, where spring is just beginning. When we were in India, we heard that spring was arriving early this year. However, upon our arrival here, it seemed to be progressing quite slowly. Normally, by the end of April, cherry trees, pear trees, and apple trees are in full bloom, and various wildflowers surround the landscape. This year, though, aside from the anemones and the bright yellow carpet of dandelions and marsh marigold, there are only a few blossoms available. Most trees are still waiting for their leaves to bud, and some beech trees are just starting to sprout. The lingering effects of last year's cyclone, Amy, are still felt in the forest. We went to visit the Brunelness Forest, where the white anemones bloom like a beautiful white carpet—an ideal spot for a lovely walk among the tiny flowers. However, we were disappointed to see broken trees scattered throughout the forest, which created quite a mess and made it less enjoyable for photography. We then headed towards Helgeroa Road and were delighted to see the greenery there. Some trees have developed soft, beautiful green leaves, enhancing the landscape's charm. The Brunalaness didn't appear very interesting. The forest has lost many trees from last year's Amy hurricane, making it look quite sparse. This is not a very good feeling, but we couldn't have control over nature. But as we headed towards Helgeroa road, things changed very quickly. The view of green, lush trees with soft leaves, those flowers of anemone, dandelion, and marsh marigold, gave us a happy smile. ![](https://images.ecency.com/DQmaNG7VKxitqMEk439o3os4tGUdXPMFYUenFzeaUNUXMMt/20260502_111422.jpg) The lush greenery of the forest was truly refreshing for the mind. After spending some time playing with the flowers and taking pictures, we continued toward Larvik. My husband was driving while I captured the scenery through my camera. Each time we visit, experiencing the natural beauty here feels unique and delightful. The Bridge over the River Logan on E18 highway, and the view of the Silver Sea from Longestrand Hill is stunning. As soon as we reached the Bøkeskogen forest, after seeing the condition of the forest, we were again emotional. The forest, which was full of trees, had become very sparse, Amy's feat. ![](https://images.ecency.com/DQmeQksmFs8wYAxi7rfVH1tHeK6MUcb5qDVPq4Thj3yRJUH/p1060295.jpg) ![](https://images.ecency.com/DQmU6362Qe9pd4bWf2GhtmKazfaBAgkELBHkZnbrwdKBcDP/p1060235.jpg) These two photos are from a couple of years back; this was the condition of Bøkeskogen exactly on 13 May, when we were walking there. But we continued our walk, and finding some good spots, were content with whatever was available and seeking the best. We couldn't find a lush of anemone flowers, normally it blooms every year, or the very green feeling while walking around. Last year's damage was unforgettable, which is an example to see in the spring. But after walking around, we came across the other part of the forest. It is nice and green and has not much damage here. ![](https://images.ecency.com/DQmYxUeDTxKPg6vyiSpL7o4FmJBcP4rbwp15nev1tvbw3zG/20260502_120429.jpg) ![](https://images.ecency.com/DQmQaHWqDRiyp1BWuHU5VYdArwbDcq9HPiLBrDqLgX4MZ6F/20260502_120547.jpg) ![](https://images.ecency.com/DQmZdh3EfJc7mr34667ZHbjYEDf8YGH8JSBihwAt5QPBeVc/20260502_120606.jpg) After exploring this part of the forest, we felt very happy. After spending some time in the greenery and fresh air, we headed back home. This was my Wednesday walk from Brunnala to Helgeroa and Bøkeskogen. I'm pleased to share this experience with you through the community initiative #WednesdayWalk by @tattoodjay. Thank you very much! [//]:# ([//]:# (!worldmappin 59.06092 lat 10.03265 long d3scr))

But don’t we all? Because our sense of control is directly tied to our sense of certainty. And who wants to be uncertain? We want to be sure about a lot of things, especially when it comes to our lives. We want to know (for sure) if our money is enough. If we don’t have this worry, then it is because we are certain we have enough. We want to know (for sure) if our time is enough. If our efforts are enough. If other people like us enough. If we are good enough. If we are enough. To have certainty over these things means we can relinquish our worries about them. And until we can become certain, we do all sorts of things trying to control the outcomes, the situations, and even other people. But just as the above quote says (it’s from a book I read a few months back), to be moved and be delighted by other people or a work of art means we have to let go of full control. -----

A Moment in a Museum

----- ![1.jpg](https://images.hive.blog/DQmPvT1fbc54EnMb7bGoFpF8jYW8LCtnCSZcFr5sGWjA9fd/1.jpg) So now I’m going to share about my last day in Auckland, where I allowed myself to let go of full control, and how I found delight in it. I had no idea where we were headed. I was already quite satisfied that I was walking around Auckland. The entire city was a tourist attraction for me already. Turns out, she was taking me to the Auckland Art Gallery. She told me it was free, and that was all I needed to know. We climbed up a short hill to get to the museum. It was a massive building. Usually, a wrong turn or a missed stop would feel like a loss of control, a crack in the certainty of the itinerary. But that afternoon, the uncertainty was just part of the experience. The bus eventually came, the restaurant was found, and the meal was hearty. Everything worked out without me having to exert control over it. I got to savor my last day in New Zealand and for a few hours that day, I had no questions about whether money was enough, whether time was enough, or if I was doing enough. I was just there to be delighted by the moment. Good bye Auckland, see you again.

Half of my portfolio is now ZEC.

That's not a hedge. That's not a trade I'm planning to exit. That's a conviction bet, and I want to walk through how I got here, because the path mattered more than the destination.

I started with a little bit. I bought some, told myself it was exposure. Then I started learning more.

## How a "Little Bit" Turned into 50%

I felt like the technology was a lot more deep than it appeared on the surface.

All the times I heard about Zcash over the years, I never really gave it a real look. Not until we integrated it into [LeoDex](https://leodex.io). That's the thing about walking the factory floor. You can't see what's actually there until you're inside building.

Once I started working with my team on Zcash and ZEC, I started learning about everything Zcash offered. Transparent cash you can spend onchain. Shielded cash. **Private digital onchain money.**

The privacy narrative never excited me a whole lot to begin with. I love privacy as much as the next guy, but onchain capital was what I had more of an interest in. Learning about ZEC opened my eyes to a very different view about what "private onchain money" truly means. More on that later.

The flow of moving between transparent and private money. Actually spendable, actually usable in the real world is what really started to excite me.

![image](https://img.leopedia.io/DQmUAHT3Wa9HR9PQdTKqtTRHGJswh4XNkVmi3pn4ypWgt54/image.png)

*shielding ZEC inside the LeoDex Desktop Wallet*

The shielding flow led me down a deep rabbit hole on what Zcash could offer both now and in the future. I saw technology, updates, and community spirit behind Zcash that I had never seen before.

Once we started adding it to LeoDex and tweeting about it and talking about it, we started getting a lot of people involved. They started telling me more about Zcash.

I started making friends in the community. Learning more. **That's how the sizing decision grew from a little bit into 50%.**

It wasn't a single moment. It was a thousand small ones that compounded.

## The 180 on Privacy I Never Saw Coming

I have to admit my entire perspective did a 180.

Two years ago, I was as guilty as everyone else. **Thinking the use cases for privacy didn't go much beyond the anecdotal dogmas about privacy coins just being used to hide transactions.**

I thought of the communities behind privacy coins as undigestible to the rest of the world. I figured privacy coins would never really take off. So I focused more on Bitcoin.

I still have a lot of Bitcoin. I still believe in Bitcoin very fervently.

But my narrative around my portfolio has shifted. **Bitcoin is the gold standard, the gold bar I put in my vault, and Zcash is onchain private digital cash I can spend at any time, for anything, anywhere**, and I can use features that let me instantly pay and settle in other cryptos but use shielded ZEC when I want to pay for them.

Inb4 people say "well if its spendable cash, why own it and not just buy it to use it when you need it?" Betting on the technology growing is another aspect of holding ZEC and that's why many of us buy it and HODL it instead of just spending all the ZEC we have. There's two sides to this framing.

Spending ZEC is effectively the same as using physical cash in the real world.

Sometimes you just want to use physical cash to pay for something. Simple, clean, private. **Easy**!!

The Zcash ecosystem and community do something really well. They make Zcash extremely friendly. **Private digital onchain money, not about hiding activities, but maintaining the level of privacy you'd have in the real world spending physical cash.**

That reframe is the major 180 right there. It's something that institutional investors, companies and hedge funds (potentially even banks, one day) can get behind. It's less about "hiding" and more about "natural free rights".

Then AI showed up and changed my perspective even more.

AI agents tend to prefer quickly settling onchain money that also has privacy. If an agent is working on a project, they don't necessarily want to be public, but they need to pay for API or inference or other things. They'd rather use a form of cash that can't be linked directly to what they're working on.

That's just one niche use case.

Expand it outward. **You don't want your health insurance company knowing you went and bought donuts yesterday, because they might raise your insurance costs.**

Ten years ago that sounded dystopian. Today it sounds like a Q3 product roadmap.

**You use your iPhone, you have a conversation with a friend about local burrito shops, and suddenly you're getting all these ads for local burrito shops.**

We're already in an era of rampant oversight. **The leap from where we are now to companies using our spending habits to negatively impact us is not a big leap, and it's probably already happening in some parts of the world.**

That's what's going to change how people view things like Zcash.

## Walking the Factory Floor on Zcash

![image](https://img.leopedia.io/DQmYaoG4cEnga3hVVxQ3Ff5fgkeVuea9RwXHn6Vp5CpA9Gw/image.png)

The privacy wallet we're building on LeoDex isn't a clone of what already exists.

What we're going for is an intensely normalized user experience. Really focused on the average user's ability to actually use Zcash, but still extremely technically capable. More technically capable than any other Zcash wallet out there.

The LeoDex team does this really well. We hide the hard parts of UI behind permission gates. A user can easily do the surface-level things, and as they want to get deeper, they follow a nice progression into deeper features.

We've learned this over basically ten years in the crypto space.

That's the unique thing we bring. **Usability. User-friendliness. Clean UX and UI.**

The reason nobody else is building it isn't really a technical or regulatory wall. It's that **the bigger players don't have the design DNA to make a privacy product feel approachable, and the existing privacy communities have been content to build for crypto-natives**, not for the average person.

That gap is wide open and [LeoDex](https://leodex.io) intends to fill it. 

## Why ZEC Sits in the Middle, and Why that Matters

Here's the part that took me longest to see.

Zcash actually lives right in the middle. Somewhere between the digital-gold narrative and Monero. That's really important to grasp.

Zcash is very digestible. Something like Monero is harder to digest, especially the community around it.

I'm not a Monero hater. Monero has an important place in the marketplace. It's just different than Zcash.

**Zec has reached this Bitcoin level of pureness, and that purity is what's going to take Zcash into the number-two spot in terms of being one of the largest cryptos in the world** and utilized heavily on a day-to-day basis by the average person.

Zec has a lot more overlap with something like Bitcoin, but acting more as cash versus Bitcoin acting like gold.

The reason the market has been pricing ZEC wrong for years is exactly this. **Everyone, including me until recently, fit Zcash into either the digital-gold bucket (where Bitcoin currently sits) or the hardcore-privacy bucket (where Monero currently sits).**

Realizing it doesn't belong in either bucket but **creates a category of its own** is the real mindset shift.

**It's the digestible, spendable, AI-era cash layer that sits between them. That's the critical narrative.**

People ask, why Zcash in particular?

Zcash has a uniquely positioned institutional acceptedness because it can be both transparent and shielded. **A lot of people point at that as a flaw, but it's actually a feature. You can have both.**

What needs to happen on regulation and macro is pretty much the status quo just needs to keep happening. Winklevoss Twins x Gemini adopted it heavily. Naval and other top VC investors got in the trenches. Now Grayscale wants a ZEC ETF. Tomorrow, Ray Dalio may start buying and propagandizing ZEC. 

The natural progression of AI. The natural progression of onchain settlement. The natural progression of people getting tired of surveillance capitalism. That's the tailwind.

The proof point is the price of Zcash going up is directly correlated with all these factors combining at this critical moment.

AI taking a large hold in society. Onchain private money handling that. Zcash uniquely positioned in branding, community, ecosystem, and technology.

I'm not waiting for permission from the market to be right.

Half my stack is in ZEC because the next five years of crypto don't belong to whoever has the loudest narrative. They belong to whoever has the most usable answer to a question every human is about to start asking.

Stop fitting ZEC into the wrong bucket and start paying attention.

When you're ready to start taking ZEC seriously, my team and I are actively building in the crosschain space. We were the first DEX Interface to launch Zcash DEX trading for Maya Protocol and Near Intents. We're now building an entire privacy-centric wallet that lives on your device and lets you hold, buy, swap and pay using Shielded ZEC. We're calling our payment rails "AnyPay" where you can pay shielded ZEC and the receiver gets **any** crypto as the output. Private onchain digital cash is now a reality.
